checks.prompt: A logistics company runs a route-planning agent built in one framework, a customs-paperwork agent bought from a vendor and running in that vendor's cloud, and an internal invoicing agent. They want the route planner to hand shipments to the customs agent and then to invoicing. The vendor will not expose the customs agent's prompts, memory or tool list, and a customs filing can take hours. Which property of this protocol makes it the right fit, and which is a distraction here?
checks.explanation: Two design commitments make this the right layer. Participants are deliberately black boxes — they advertise what they can do, never how — which is exactly what lets two organisations collaborate without either giving up its intellectual property or its security boundary. And long-running work is native: progress arrives as a stream of updates, or through a registered callback, rather than as one blocking call. What is not in scope is how any individual agent reaches its own tools and data; that is a separate protocol at a lower layer, and the two stack rather than compete.
options: The fit is that participants stay opaque — collaboration happens entirely through advertised capabilities, work orders and returned results, so the vendor shares nothing internal — combined with first-class support for work that runs for hours through streaming updates and callbacks. The distraction is anything about how each agent reaches its own tools and data, which is a different layer entirely

The fit is that it gives every participant a shared memory and a common tool registry, so the route planner can inspect what the customs agent knows before delegating; the hours-long filing is handled by keeping the HTTP connection open for the duration
The fit is purely the encoding: standardising on one message envelope removes the custom glue, and the opacity and duration questions are deployment concerns the protocol takes no position on
The fit is that it replaces the three agents with one orchestrator process, which is what removes the integration glue; opacity then follows because there is only one agent left

checks.prompt: Explain this protocol using the contractor analogy, naming what each element of the analogy corresponds to. Then use the analogy to explain why a client that treats every request as a single blocking call — send the work, expect the answer back — will break on any non-trivial job, and what the protocol offers instead.
checks.expected: A correct answer must map the analogy onto the protocol's elements. Finding a contractor by reading their business card is discovery: a JSON document at a conventional well-known URL declaring the agent's name, endpoint, version, the skills it offers, what it supports (streaming, callbacks) and how to authenticate — read and vetted BEFORE anything is sent. Handing over a work order is the durable unit of work, identified by an id and holding state on the remote side. Progress reports are streamed status updates. Deliverables are the outputs the remote agent produces, made of the same content parts messages are made of. Never seeing inside the workshop is opacity: no access to the other side's memory, tools or prompt. The one-shot failure must be explained through that state: the unit of work is stateful and lives on the server, and a real job frequently pauses in a state meaning more input is needed — the agent parks the work and waits for an answer. A client that treats the send as one-shot either drops the parked work or, worse, sends the answer as a brand-new request, so the original never resumes and the follow-up has no context. What the protocol offers instead is referencing the same work order by its id across turns, reading its current state on demand after a reconnect, subscribing to a stream of updates, re-attaching to that stream if the connection drops, and registering a callback for work too long to sit and watch. Noting that this multi-turn statefulness is precisely what distinguishes it from a single stateless tool call is a plus.

checks.prompt: An agent must accept a scanned invoice image plus a structured JSON record describing the vendor, and return both a plain-text summary and a machine-readable extraction. A developer proposes serialising everything to text, because 'the transport is JSON-RPC over HTTP so text is all it can carry'. What does the protocol's content model actually provide, and how do the two directions differ?
checks.explanation: The atomic content unit is the part, and there are three kinds: text, a file (bytes or a URI), and structured data. That is what makes the protocol modality-agnostic — an image or a JSON record travels as what it is. The distinction the developer is missing is the container: an inbound turn from either side is a message, and an output the remote agent produces is an artifact. Both are made of the same parts, and both may carry several, so a text summary and a structured extraction can come back together.
options: Content is carried as parts, of which there are three kinds — plain text, a file given as bytes or a URI, and structured data — so the image and the JSON record travel as themselves rather than stringified. Both directions use those same parts, but they sit in different containers: an inbound turn is a message, while what the remote agent produces is an artifact, and both may carry several parts
Only text is carried in messages; files and structured data must be uploaded out of band first and referenced by URL in a text part, which is why artifacts exist as a separate concept
Parts are an inbound-only concept for messages; results always come back as a single text blob, so the machine-readable extraction has to be re-parsed by the client
Content is untyped JSON and the three part kinds are only labels the client may set for its own use, so the developer is right that serialising everything to text is equivalent

checks.prompt: Implement `run_agent(requests, vocabulary)`, the stateful half of a remote agent — one server-side task store processing a list of JSON-RPC 2.0 requests in order. `vocabulary` maps a known lowercase phrase to its translation. Return the list of responses, each `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": <request id>, ...}` with exactly one of `"result"` or `"error"`, an error being `{"code": int, "message": str}`. A task is `{"id", "contextId", "status", "artifacts", "history"}` where `status` is at least `{"state": ...}`. Handle three methods. `message/send` takes `params["message"]` (`{"role", "parts"}`) and an OPTIONAL `params["taskId"]`: with no `taskId`, create a task with id `"task-1"`, `"task-2"`, … in creation order and `contextId` `"ctx-N"` to match; with one, resume that stored task. Append the message to `history`, then read the phrase by joining the `text` of the parts whose `kind` is `"text"` (ignore other kinds), lowercased and stripped of surrounding spaces, full stops and quotes. A known phrase completes the task: append an artifact `{"artifactId": "art-N", "name": "translation", "parts": [{"kind": "text", "text": <translation>}]}` numbered from 1 within that task and set the state to `"completed"` with no other status keys. An unknown phrase parks it: set the state to `"input-required"` and put a `"message"` on the status with `"role": "agent"` and a text part asking for a known phrase, adding no artifact. Return the task. `tasks/get` takes `params["id"]` and returns the stored task. `tasks/cancel` takes `params["id"]` and sets the state to `"canceled"`. A `taskId` or `id` naming no stored task is error -32001; resuming or cancelling a task already in a terminal state (`completed`, `failed`, `canceled`) is error -32002; any other method is -32601. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The assertions are aimed at the one property that separates this from a stateless call: the unit of work is durable and is resumed by id. Watch the pair of cases in the middle. Answering the agent's question WITH the task id resumes the parked work — the same id comes back, the history now holds both turns, the clarification disappears from the status and the deliverable appears. Answering WITHOUT it silently starts a second, unrelated task and leaves the first parked forever with no output, which is exactly what a client written as if every send were one-shot does. The rest guards the edges that make the state machine real: a terminal task cannot be reopened, cancellation is a transition rather than a deletion and is itself refused once terminal, and reading the task back reports what the last turn left there. Note too that only the text parts are read: a structured part travelling alongside them is content for the agent, not something to stringify into the phrase.
checks.test:
VOCAB = {"hello": "bonjour", "goodbye": "au revoir", "yes": "oui"}


def say(text, task_id=None, rid=1):
    params = {"message": {"role": "user",
                          "parts": [{"kind": "text", "text": text}]}}
    if task_id is not None:
        params["taskId"] = task_id
    return {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "method": "message/send", "params": params}


def get(task_id, rid=2):
    return {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "method": "tasks/get", "params": {"id": task_id}}


# A phrase the agent cannot handle parks the task rather than failing it, and the
# clarification it needs rides on the status, not on an artifact.
first = run_agent([say("see you later")], VOCAB)[0]["result"]
assert first["status"]["state"] == "input-required", first
assert first["artifacts"] == [], first
assert first["status"]["message"]["role"] == "agent", first
assert len(first["history"]) == 1, first
tid = first["id"]

# The multi-turn round trip: the SAME task is resumed by id, not replaced.
session = run_agent([say("see you later"), say("goodbye", task_id="task-1", rid=3)], VOCAB)
resumed = session[1]["result"]
assert resumed["id"] == "task-1", resumed
assert resumed["status"]["state"] == "completed", resumed
assert len(resumed["history"]) == 2, resumed
assert resumed["artifacts"][0]["parts"][0]["text"] == "au revoir", resumed
assert "message" not in resumed["status"], resumed

# ...and the state is durable: a later read of the same id reports it, which is what
# lets a client reconnect instead of holding the turn open.
polled = run_agent([say("see you later"), say("goodbye", task_id="task-1", rid=3),
                    get("task-1", rid=4)], VOCAB)[2]["result"]
assert polled["status"]["state"] == "completed", polled
assert polled["artifacts"][0]["parts"][0]["text"] == "au revoir", polled

# Answering WITHOUT the id starts a second task and leaves the first parked -- the
# failure mode of treating the send as one-shot.
split = run_agent([say("see you later"), say("goodbye", rid=3), get("task-1", rid=4)], VOCAB)
assert split[1]["result"]["id"] != "task-1", split[1]
assert split[2]["result"]["status"]["state"] == "input-required", split[2]
assert split[2]["result"]["artifacts"] == [], split[2]

# A finished task is finished: continuing it is refused, not silently reopened.
closed = run_agent([say("hello"), say("yes", task_id="task-1", rid=3)], VOCAB)
assert closed[0]["result"]["status"]["state"] == "completed", closed[0]
assert "error" in closed[1] and closed[1]["error"]["code"] == -32002, closed[1]

# Cancellation is a state transition on the stored task, and only from a live one.
cancelled = run_agent([say("see you later"),
                       {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tasks/cancel",
                        "params": {"id": "task-1"}},
                       get("task-1", rid=4),
                       {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 5, "method": "tasks/cancel",
                        "params": {"id": "task-1"}}], VOCAB)
assert cancelled[1]["result"]["status"]["state"] == "canceled", cancelled[1]
assert cancelled[2]["result"]["status"]["state"] == "canceled", cancelled[2]
assert "error" in cancelled[3], cancelled[3]
assert "error" in run_agent([say("see you later", task_id="task-9")], VOCAB)[0]

# Unknown ids and unknown methods are protocol errors with distinct codes.
missing = run_agent([get("task-404")], VOCAB)[0]
assert "error" in missing and missing["error"]["code"] == -32001, missing
other = run_agent([{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tasks/resubscribe",
                    "params": {"id": "task-1"}}], VOCAB)[0]
assert "error" in other and other["error"]["code"] == -32601, other

# Every response is a well-formed envelope carrying its request's id.
envelopes = run_agent([say("hello", rid=11), get("task-1", rid=12)], VOCAB)
assert [r["id"] for r in envelopes] == [11, 12], envelopes
for response in envelopes:
    assert response["jsonrpc"] == "2.0", response
    assert ("result" in response) != ("error" in response), response

# Only the text parts are read, so a structured part alongside them is not stringified
# into the phrase.
mixed = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "message/send", "params": {
    "message": {"role": "user", "parts": [{"kind": "text", "text": "hello"},
                                          {"kind": "data", "data": {"tone": "formal"}}]}}}
assert run_agent([mixed], VOCAB)[0]["result"]["status"]["state"] == "completed"

checks.prompt: A client integration is failing three ways. It sends every follow-up as a brand-new request, so clarifications never resume the original work. It calls the state-reading method in a tight loop against an agent whose discovery document advertises support for incremental delivery. And it passes the remote agent's returned text straight into its own model's context unfiltered. Which set of corrections is right?
checks.explanation: Three independent mistakes. The unit of work is stateful, so continuity comes from referring to it by id — not from a held-open connection and not from the server guessing. Capabilities are advertised so the client can use the efficient path: when incremental delivery is offered, subscribe to it or register a callback, rather than hammering the state-reading method. And a remote agent is untrusted code on the other end of a network: its messages and outputs enter your model's context, so they are potentially adversarial exactly as any other external content is. Authentication is necessary but answers none of the three.
options: Reference the existing work order by its id across turns, persist those work orders and re-attach to a dropped stream rather than restarting; subscribe to the incremental stream (or register a callback for very long jobs) instead of polling; and treat everything coming back as untrusted input, because the remote side is code you do not control and its text can carry an injection

Sending each follow-up fresh is correct because the protocol is stateless by design; polling is the supported mechanism and the advertised streaming flag is only a hint; and returned content is safe because it was produced by an agent rather than by a user

The follow-up problem is fixed by keeping one HTTP connection open for the whole conversation; polling is fine at any rate as long as it is authenticated; and injection is not a concern here because it only applies to tool servers, not to peer agents
All three are symptoms of missing authentication: once the client authenticates, the server can associate the follow-ups itself, throttle the polling, and vouch for the content it returns

checks.prompt: A single team owns a research agent and a drafting agent that run in one process, share a state object and are orchestrated by a graph framework. A colleague proposes putting this protocol between them 'for consistency', since the team also uses it to reach a partner's compliance agent. Argue whether that is a good idea, be specific about what it would cost inside a monolith and what it would buy, and then explain the relationship between this protocol and the one that connects an agent to its tools and data.
checks.expected: A correct answer must argue against adopting it inside the single process and be concrete about the trade. Inside one framework and one process the two agents already share state and are orchestrated directly; the protocol's machinery — an HTTP hop, a durable work-order lifecycle with server-side state, discovery documents, authentication and an envelope for every turn — buys nothing there, because there is no cross-vendor interop to gain and no trust or intellectual-property boundary to preserve. Its value comes precisely from crossing an ownership or framework boundary, which is why the partner's compliance agent IS a correct use. A strong answer notes that the shared state object, which makes the in-process orchestration simple, is the very thing the protocol's opacity forbids, so 'consistency' would mean giving up a real capability; and that when you find yourself needing the other agent's internals, that is the signal the boundary is in the wrong place or the agents should be merged. The relationship between the two protocols must be stated as complementary layers rather than alternatives: this one is agent-to-agent delegation, the other gives one agent access to tools, data and prompt templates, and they stack — an agent reached over this protocol commonly uses the other one internally to reach its own tools. Noting that frameworks increasingly speak this protocol at their edges while staying native inside, so the two are not exclusive, is a plus.
